blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12Δ^\top FΔ$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $α^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.

MOE模型在小扰动时显示出非夸张反应,缩放为$ 0.63}. bf16中的计算每序列梯度可导致4倍的预测错误. 我们用fp32来追踪这些出错,然后在后行的下半部进行算术,并消除这些出错。 批量-内核以0.55倍的吞吐量运行,而还原顺序的变化引入了每序列0.17-0.22纳特的下限. 我们建造一个屏幕,上面有一条流式的fp32 Fisher通道, 并用一个带子来修剪收音机的预言, 标出一个对齐的收音机和每层格式分配的旗帜。 在看不见的Mistral-7B-v0.3家族中,所有6个预测都属于波段,所有3个KL预算都得到满足,而vLLM吞吐量预测在0.4%。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
An LLM serving stack now picks a weight format for every model and deployment: int8 or fp8 where quality matters most, int4 with a
group size where memory binds, block-scaled 4-bit formats [ 22 ] and, on new GPUs, stochastic instead of nearest
rounding [ 12 ] . Measuring task quality for every combination is slow, so a screen that predicts the damage from the
unquantized model is attractive. The standard one is second order: the KL divergence between a model and its quantized copy is
approximately 1 2 ​ Δ ⊤ ​ F ​ Δ \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta^{\top}F\Delta , with F F the Fisher information and Δ \Delta the weight perturbation. It costs one
forward and backward pass per calibration sequence, after which every candidate format is a dot product per tensor; Hessian-aware bit
allocation [ 7 ] and second-order post-training quantizers [ 9 , 11 , 21 ] build on the same expansion.

blocks.en:
A screen is used in two ways. It ranks candidates on a fixed calibration set, and it gives an absolute number that is
compared with a quality budget. We test both, together with the implementation choices that decide whether the number can be trusted:
the precision of the per-sequence gradients, the estimator over sequences, and the noise floor of the engine that measures the KL. The
question is one of linear response: the quantized model is a perturbed copy, and the KL is its quadratic response in the Fisher metric
(§ 3 ). Every decision rule was frozen—predictions, scorers and file checksums—before its GPU run, and the models
added after Qwen3-8B played no part in developing the analysis. The ledger in the supplementary material lists every batch with its frozen prediction
and outcome.

blocks.en: 3 Theory: linear response in the Fisher metric
blocks.zh: 3个 理论:Fisher 度量法中的线性反应

blocks.en:
The expansion KL ≈ 1 2 ​ Δ ⊤ ​ F ​ Δ \mathrm{KL}\approx\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta^{\top}F\Delta is the quadratic response of the model’s output distribution to a
perturbation of its parameters, with the Fisher information as the metric. Four things can break it, and the paper tests each. First,
the response is a sum over sequences of a quadratic form, and that sum can be dominated by rare configurations: a heavy tail makes the
mean not self-averaging, while ratios on a fixed sample set remain accurate (§ 4 , § 5 ). Second, the adjoint
dynamics that produce the per-sequence gradients can be unstable in reduced precision and amplify a rounding error on its way back through the layers; the blow-up is then a
property of the backward pass, not of the model, and in our data a single layer supplies the step that separates blow-ups from controls (§ 6 ). Third, the perturbation
can leave the quadratic regime, which an α \alpha scan detects as a higher-order term (§ 7 ). Fourth, the diagonal
estimator treats the rounding errors of a tensor as sign-incoherent along the gradient; when they are coherent it under-predicts by a
factor that does not close as α → 0 \alpha\to 0 (§ 8 ). Rounding also supplies a
quenched/annealed pair: round-to-nearest is a fixed (quenched) error for a given input and stochastic rounding an annealed one, and the
variance term of the expansion predicts their ratio. The run-to-run floor of a bf16 engine is this layer’s thermal noise: any change of
reduction order realises a new rounding configuration of the same size (§ 9 ).

in fp32 alone leave 0.09 and 0.11 of the error at the median, but each fails on a different sequence), so a practical recipe keeps
the whole lower half of the backward in fp32.

blocks.en: 9 Determinism has a price, and the noise floor is one number

blocks.en:
Numerical mismatch is only meaningful above the run-to-run noise floor of the serving engine. vLLM’s batch-invariant mode removes that
noise by fixing reduction order; on GH200 at 32 concurrent requests it ran at 0.55 × \times the throughput of the default mode.
blocks.zh:

噪声通过固定还原令;在32个同时请求的GH200上,它运行在0.55×\时间默认模式的吞吐量上.

blocks.en:
We measured that floor on GH200 with a frozen criterion (teacher-forced Qwen3-8B, 256 samples of 768 tokens): every comparison in which
the reduction order differs—other kernel selections, two- or four-way tensor parallelism, batch-invariant against default
kernels—gave 0.17–0.22 nats per sequence (the 4 pre-registered comparisons: 0.17–0.21), the same
as on H100, while reruns that reuse the kernel selection were bitwise identical. The batch size itself barely matters: reading the same
autotune cache, 8 and 256 concurrent sequences agree on 99.3% of the token log-probabilities (KL 0.000). Because
the autotuned kernel selection was shared within the run, the floor is best read as that of an independent bf16 rounding
realisation, set by which kernels run rather than by how requests are batched. KL measured across engine instances or configurations
carries this floor, so differences below about 0.2 nats per sequence between such measurements are not resolvable unless the kernel
selection is fixed; batch-invariant kernels cost 0.81 × \times throughput in this teacher-forced setting.

block terms are largest on the calibration sequences , so the layers left at int4 are, by selection, ones whose terms came out low

both uniform integer cells; that prediction failed: they came out at 1.06–1.08, below int8 and int4
(1.11 and 1.12). A post-hoc bootstrap—resample the sequences, re-allocate, evaluate each chosen configuration on
the full sample—puts the optimism at 1.16–1.44 × \times with eight sequences, matching the smoke run, and at
1.015–1.022 × \times with 256. A screener that allocates on its
own calibration set needs a few hundred sequences, or a held-out split for the final prediction.

blocks.en:
Four dense models from two families (4B–32B) and one mixture-of-experts model, whose pre-registered test is inconclusive (the
dense control failed) and is reported as an observation; three schemes; one GPU type; sample sets of 256–512 sequences. The screener was tested on one further dense model, from a third family (Mistral-7B-v0.3). No tensor was flagged on it and
the element-diagonal form also landed in the band, so the case for the flag and the tensor-block form rests on the archived
Qwen3-32B cell; at 32 concurrent requests the three budgeted configurations gained only 4–8%
throughput over bf16 (uniform int4 17%), too small for the ± 10 % \pm 10\% throughput criterion to discriminate. The localization of the 32B int4 miss to one tensor is post hoc and rests on one
model; a weight-side explanation was refuted; a pre-registered follow-up confirmed the tensor’s role and the effect of
stochastic rounding but missed its trimmed band (verdict mixed), and the two-column localization is post hoc. The trimming fraction was chosen on Qwen3-8B and tested on the other three models only. The bf16 error is made in the
lower half of the backward (one model, four sequences); the responsible block varies by sequence, and its link to massive activations
rests on two models. Higher-order terms were measured only for OLMo-2 int4 and Qwen3-8B (set A). The original experiment’s data were not re-analysed.

blocks.en:
The expansion we test underlies pruning from Optimal Brain Damage and Optimal Brain
Surgeon [ 17 , 13 ] to WoodFisher [ 25 ] , Hessian- and Fisher-guided mixed-precision allocation
(HAQ [ 29 ] , Q-BERT [ 24 ] , HAWQ and its successors [ 7 , 6 , 31 ] ), and the
layer- and block-wise second-order objectives of post-training quantizers (AdaRound [ 21 ] , BRECQ [ 19 ] ,
OBC and GPTQ [ 9 , 11 ] ); SqueezeLLM [ 14 ] weights its codebook by a diagonal Fisher. These
methods use the expansion to choose a quantization. We test it as a predictor of the KL a fixed quantization induces, on
models fixed in advance, and find where its diagonal form fails. The Fisher we estimate is the one along Δ \Delta from sampled continuations,
the natural-gradient metric [ 1 ] , not the empirical Fisher whose limits are discussed by [ 16 ] .

(HAQ [29]、Q-BERT [24]、HAWQ及其继任者[7、6、31]),

blocks.en:
Activation-aware and outlier-aware methods—LLM.int8() [ 4 ] , SmoothQuant [ 30 ] ,
AWQ [ 20 ] , OWQ [ 18 ] , SpQR [ 5 ] , OmniQuant [ 23 ] —and rotation or
vector codebooks (QuIP, QuIP#, AQLM [ 3 , 28 , 8 ] ) protect a few channels or spread their
error. Outlier dimensions [ 15 , 2 ] , massive activations [ 26 ] and single
“super weights” [ 32 ] show that a handful of coordinates carry a model’s behaviour. Our 32B finding is of this kind
but in the error, not the weights: two input channels of one tensor whose rounding errors align with the gradient, invisible to every
weight statistic we computed.

removes, which every KL comparison between engine runs carries.
